title: Manifest Mailing System Retired
summary:
Two federal moves are on the way: the Postal Service will retire its paper-based manifest mailing system and shift mailers to electronic tools by April 1, 2026, and the Environmental Protection Agency approved part of Utah’s plan to prevent its ozone pollution from affecting other states under the 2008 standard.

For mailers, the Postal Service’s change means moving from paper manifests and hard-copy paperwork to online documentation, barcodes, and electronic payment and acceptance. Many businesses could benefit from faster processing, fewer errors, and better tracking. Small businesses in particular may find the free, web-based Intelligent Mail for Small Business Tool helpful because it doesn’t require any software and guides users step by step. Package shippers can use the Postal Service’s online shipping programs instead of paper manifests. The winners here are mailers ready to digitize and the Postal Service, which gains efficiency and more consistent data. Those who could feel the pain are small or low-tech operations that still rely on paper or legacy workflows. They may face setup time, training needs, and process changes, even with support tools available.

On air quality, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized approval of Utah’s plan to show that pollution from within the state does not prevent other states from meeting the 2008 ozone standard. Utah’s air agency supported the move, noting the long path to get here, while one anonymous commenter urged rejection out of concern for local air. The agency said this action only addresses the 2008 standard and does not add new federal requirements beyond Utah’s plan. The beneficiaries are neighboring states that rely on regional cooperation to protect public health, and Utah businesses and regulators who gain regulatory clarity after years of back-and-forth. Those who might feel negatively affected are residents and advocates who believe more aggressive action is needed on ozone, as well as any sources that may still face compliance obligations under the state plan.

Bottom line: the Postal Service is accelerating its digital shift, and the Environmental Protection Agency is closing a chapter in a long-running interstate ozone issue. Both actions aim for modernization and certainty, with real transition challenges that will need practical support to avoid leaving people behind.
